Following an enfranchisement to acquire the freehold of the building and conversion to commonhold, the former freeholder of the block will lose the freehold of the whole block but can elect or be required to retain the freehold of each of the commonhold units held by a non-consenting leaseholder and become the unit owner. They will be entitled to continue to collect any ground rent payable for that unit.

The non-consenting leaseholder will lose the right to extend their lease and instead if they wished to address their depreciating lease, they would be required to obtain the freehold of their unit and become the commonhold unit owner in place of the former freeholder of the block. At a future sale of the property, non-consenting leaseholders will be required to sell their home as a commonhold unit with the former freeholder of the block being compensated at this point.

Frequently asked questions

How will the leases of NCLs be phased out over time in a converted commonhold?

Non-consenting leaseholders may choose to buy the freehold of their commonhold unit at any point following the conversion of the wider building.

At the point of conversion, non-consenting leaseholders will lose the right to extend their lease. Instead, to address a depreciating lease they would be required to buy the freehold of their commonhold unit. This means that non-consenting leaseholders whose lease is becoming shorter will have to acquire the freehold of their unit as commonhold, instead of extending it. The Bill sets out the process for exercising this right to buy the freehold of the commonhold unit.

In addition, when non-consenting leaseholders want to sell their flat, they will need to sell it as a commonhold unit. As part of the sales process, the non-consenting leaseholder’s lease will be bought out and the freeholder will be entitled to compensation in exchange for the acquisition of the freehold. Any intermediate landlords of the lease being sold may be entitled to a share of the purchase price.

The full mechanism for selling the commonhold unit to a third-party will be set out in regulations, and will follow a similar process as for the acquisition of the commonhold unit which is set out in Schedule 3 to the Bill. For example, these regulations will provide that the price payable on the sale of a commonhold unit will be determined in the same way as it is for the right to acquire the unit, and is to be calculated in accordance with the valuation provisions for enfranchisement under the LFRA 2024.

Will measures to phase out NCLs’ leases cost leaseholders money and leave them out of pocket (e.g. force them to spend money they can’t recoup on re-sale, or be more costly than a lease extension)?

No, the cost of buying the commonhold unit will follow the process for enfranchisement and be equivalent to the cost of a lease extension, and so neither the unit holder (that is likely to be the former freeholder) nor the leaseholder will be out of pocket.

Where the non-consenting leaseholder’s flat is sold to a third-party as a commonhold unit, the former freeholder of the block would be compensated for their freehold interest at that point by taking an appropriate share of the sale proceeds. This amount will be determined by the process set out for enfranchisement and be equivalent to the amount that the leaseholder would have paid if they were instead to have bought their unit without having sold it on to a third-party.

Why will leases be phased out in a converted commonhold?

We think it is important to have a process which delivers a full commonhold over time by including a mechanism which phases out non-consenting leases.

This will give the owners the fullest flexibility to shape their commonhold without the need to have regard to non-consenting leaseholder leases.

It also ensures that the former freeholder of the block receives the compensation they are due for the loss of their freehold interest when the leaseholder buys them out.

What will be the process of converting a NCL’s lease to commonhold at the point of a lease extension or sale of the property? How will this work in practice?

Any flat in a commonhold block that is let to an NCL will need to be sold as a commonhold unit.

The process for acquiring the freehold of the commonhold unit is set out in Schedule 3 to the Bill. It can be initiated by the non-consenting leaseholder at any point.

The full mechanism for the leaseholder exercising their right to direct the sale of the unit to a third-party will be in regulations, and much of the detail will follow the same process as if the leaseholder were buying the unit themselves, set out in Schedule 3 to the Bill. For example, the price payable to the unit holder from the proceeds of sale will be determined in the same way, and the value of the freehold will be calculated in accordance with enfranchisement law which is being extended to apply to these new rights.

Where the unit is being sold at the leaseholder’s request, a proportion of the proceeds of sale will be shared with the existing unit owner (the former freeholder of the block) to compensate them for the loss of their freehold interest. Intermediate landlords may also be entitled to an appropriate share of the purchase price for the loss of their interest. From that point forward, the buyer will become the new unit owner and will be a member of the commonhold association.

This ensures that leases are phased out within a commonhold block and that the former freeholder of the block is fairly compensated for the loss of their interest.

Will the phasing out of NCLs’ leases cost NCLs money?

If a non-consenting leaseholder wants to buy the freehold of their commonhold unit, rather than sell it to someone else, then yes, they will be required to pay the freeholder of the unit for acquiring the freehold interest.

The cost should be equivalent to the price they would pay for extending their lease by obtaining a lease extension.

Are NCLs free-riding the commonhold, getting all the benefits but not having to pay for them?

No, for non-consenting leaseholders, the cost of conversion is delayed rather than avoided.

Non-consenting leaseholders will have to pay the cost of conversion for their unit, and this will be payable at the point they exercise their right to buy the freehold of the commonhold unit or sell it to someone else.

Up until this point, they will continue to pay any ground rent due to the unit holder (the freeholder of their unit).

Will NCLs pay less if they join the conversion later than if they participated at the outset?

Every conversion will be different, and costs will depend on the building, the interests being acquired and any factors such as the presence and amount of shared areas (such as adjoining land or a car park) or development value as part of the acquisition of the freehold. Initial participants will know the estimated cost before deciding whether to proceed.

A non-consenting leaseholder who later acquires the freehold estate in their commonhold unit will pay the price determined under the statutory valuation framework at that later point. That price will not necessarily be lower than the amount they would have paid by participating at the outset.

In particular, the price is likely to be affected by the remaining length and value of the leasehold interest at the time of acquisition; as the lease gets shorter, the price may increase.

Accommodating non-standard forms of commonhold

Micro-commonholds

The Bill introduces a mechanism for enabling smaller commonholds to vote to opt out of certain legal requirements which might be unduly onerous for them to meet. This mechanism will be provided for in secondary legislation.

Under the new commonhold framework, blocks which contain four units or fewer and no more than one non-residential unit will fall within the definition of a micro-commonhold.

In addition, a micro-commonhold should not have extensive shared areas, nor be of non-standard construction. The definition of micro-commonhold in the Bill may be amended by regulations to reflect this, and to further adapt the meaning of “micro-commonhold” in future.

It is intended that micro-commonholds will be able to adopt alternative articles of association, either at the point of registration or following a unanimous vote by owners, instead of the “default mandatory articles” otherwise applicable to all commonholds. These micro-commonhold specific articles will be set out in regulations. They will relax rules around director appointments and processes concerning meetings and votes, making it easier for very small commonholds to operate.

It is intended that micro-commonholds will also be able to adopt an alternative version of the core Commonhold Community Statement, which will provide further flexibility around how they are run. This alternative core CCS will also be set out in regulations. See parts of the guide on CCS and local rules above.

Frequently asked questions

Why are provisions being made for micro-commonholds?

This is a recognition that adopting a ‘one size fits all’ approach may not work for every type of commonhold.

In particular, we recognised that some of the rules around directors, could prove onerous for some very small commonholds and this may dissuade blocks of this type from becoming commonholds in the future.

We used the Moving to Commonhold consultation to seek views on whether micro-commonholds should be specifically recognised and how the CCS and articles could be adapted. There was good support for making specific provision about micro-commonholds.

What kind of flexibilities will micro-commonholds be granted?

Bespoke rules for micro-commonholds will be provided in an alternative, micro-commonhold specific articles of association and core CCS, which will be developed for inclusion in secondary legislation.

It is intended that micro-commonholds will be able to appoint a single director for their commonhold association, rather than the two that are required within a standard commonhold. They may also be allowed to opt out of the requirement for directors to retire at each Annual General Meeting, and to follow simplified meeting and voting arrangements.

We will keep under review the need to add, amend or withdraw any of the specified flexibilities and make further changes via regulations if necessary.

Can commonholds that include commercial units be micro-commonholds?

A micro-commonhold must have a majority of residential units (or if there are only two units, at least one must be residential). This means that a commonhold comprising one or two flats above a shop will qualify as a micro-commonhold, but more complex commonholds with multiple commercial units will be excluded.

Regulations may also be made to apply a maximum commercial floorspace to micro-commonholds. This would mean for example that three flats above a very large store would not meet the definition of a micro-commonhold.

Could a commonhold that has decided to use micro-commonhold core CCS rules and micro-commonhold articles, change its decision and revert to using the standard commonhold CCS and articles of association?

Yes, a commonhold could decide to revert back to using the default core CCS and articles, although this is not something we expect to happen often.

If a commonhold decides that it no longer wishes to use micro-commonhold articles and CCS rules, it will need to hold a vote to make that change and that vote will need to be taken by all members and be unanimously in favour of making the change.

If a commonhold changes such that it no longer meets the statutory definition of a micro-commonhold, it will cease to be a micro-commonhold and the commonhold association will have to update and lodge a revised set of CCS and articles of association to reflect this.

Mixed tenure

Registered providers of social housing are required to meet various regulatory requirements around the management and maintenance of units they own. To ensure that they are not prevented from doing this by collective decision-making in mixed-tenure commonholds which contain both owner-occupied and social homes, it is intended that commonholds with a certain proportion of social housing units will be able to adopt varied articles of association and Commonhold Community Statements on registration of a new commonhold, or if a specific proportion of unit-holders in an existing commonhold vote in favour.

The social housing-specific articles of association will strengthen providers’ ability to represent their tenants’ interests by giving them a ‘right of first refusal’ on director positions. It is also intended that the CCS will be modified to mandate compliance with relevant social housing standards enforced by the Regulator of Social Housing.

Frequently asked questions

Will these rules enable social housing providers to dominate commonhold decision-making?

No. In all but very small developments (‘micro-commonholds’), commonhold associations must have more than one director. Providers’ ‘right of first refusal’ on a director position will not affect the ability of ordinary members to become directors themselves, or to exercise a vote on key decisions such as agreeing an annual budget.

New commonholds will only be able to adopt the social housing-specific articles and CCS on registration if there are a certain proportion of social housing units within the development. In existing commonholds, commonhold association members will need to vote unanimously in order to adopt the alternative articles and CCS.

Specialist older people’s housing

Specialist older people’s housing covers a range of models, from relatively straightforward age-restricted housing to more service-led schemes providing extensive communal facilities, support services and continuing professional operator involvement.

The government recognises the important role this sector plays in providing older people with greater choice and homes that meet their changing needs. As such, our approach is tailored to different parts of the sector. First, leasehold will remain available for housing-with-care; second, commonhold will provide the right model for more straightforward forms of specialist older people’s housing; and third, we will adapt commonhold to meet the particular needs of more service-led models.

For the parts of the sector moving to commonhold, we want to retain its central benefits for consumers, including freehold ownership of individual homes, greater transparency and resident control, while ensuring it can work for more complex and service-led developments. The Bill already provides some of the flexibility needed to achieve this. The government intends to bring forward any further provisions needed later in the Bill’s passage, with further detail to be set out in secondary legislation.

In particular, for some schemes, it will be important to accommodate continuing professional operator involvement in the development. The detailed arrangements are still being developed and will need to strike an appropriate balance between supporting the effective operation of these developments and protecting the interests of residents.

The Bill will also allow regulations to make exceptions to the general prohibition on event fees in commonhold. The government intends to use this flexibility for specialist older people’s housing where event fees form part of the way in which additional services and facilities are funded and can make this type of housing more affordable for consumers. Any exception will need to be accompanied by appropriate transparency and consumer protections.

Frequently asked questions

Why does commonhold need to be adapted for specialist older people’s housing?

Some specialist older people’s housing operates differently from a conventional block of flats. Service-led schemes may include extensive communal facilities, support services and continuing professional operator involvement.

A standardised approach may not provide sufficient flexibility to support these models effectively. The government therefore intends to adapt commonhold so that it can accommodate their distinctive operational and funding arrangements.

This does not alter the fundamental principles of commonhold. Residents will own the freehold of their homes and, through the commonhold association, retain an important role in how their development is run.

Will residents still have control over their commonhold?

Yes. The objective is to preserve the central benefits of commonhold, including freehold ownership, greater transparency and resident control, while allowing proportionate professional involvement where this is needed.

The detailed arrangements are still being developed, but will need to balance the requirements of more complex, service-led specialist older people’s housing developments with appropriate transparency, resident control and consumer protections.

Why are the detailed adaptations not all included in the Bill at introduction?

The Bill already contains some of the flexibility needed to support more complex and service-led specialist older people’s housing developments as part of the wider reform of commonhold.

The government has set a clear direction that commonhold will be adapted so that it can operate effectively in specialist older people’s housing. It intends to bring forward any further provisions needed later in the Bill’s passage as the detailed arrangements are developed.

Secondary legislation will fill out the wider framework, allowing the government to work with consumers and the sector to get the detail right while retaining the fundamental benefits and protections of commonhold.

Interests in a commonhold unit

The Bill clarifies the position regarding the types of interest that can and cannot be granted out of a commonhold unit. An interest is a legal or equitable right over land or property that gives someone a degree of control or obligation in relation to it. For example, it provides that it is not possible to grant long residential leases out of commonhold units as a general rule, apart from where the lease is permitted. Currently, it is not possible to grant such leases for longer than 7 years, but this will be increased to 21 years to align with the ban on new leasehold flats.

As with the current law, it will not be possible to prevent someone from selling the whole of their commonhold unit, but a decision to sell part of a commonhold unit must meet additional requirements (such as a vote of the commonhold association). This ensures that the commonhold association maintains oversight of the process, as the creation of additional units would have implications for the distribution of voting rights and commonhold contributions. A unit owner will be free to obtain a mortgage over the whole of their unit, but will not be able to obtain a mortgage over only part of their unit.

The Bill also addresses other types of interest. The Bill creates a power for regulations to set out other types of interest that can only be granted after a vote of the association has been carried out and should not be granted out of part of a unit. For example, an interest cannot be granted out of one room of a residential unit. This prevents any complications over the ownership structure and membership of the commonhold association.

Frequently asked questions

What is an interest in land?

An interest is a legal or equitable right over land or property that gives someone a degree of control or obligation in relation to it.

This could include a freehold or leasehold estate, or a mortgage.

Changing the size or extent of a commonhold

The Bill makes it clear that a commonhold can be expanded to include new land but this must be approved unanimously by the commonhold association and the change must be reflected in a revision to its CCS. The new land must be registered before it can be added to the commonhold. For the purpose of development rights, a developer can reserve a right in the CCS that enables the developer to add land to a commonhold without a vote of the association.

If the land being added is existing commonhold land (i.e. coming from another commonhold) then both sets of directors (from both the donating commonhold association and the recipient) must certify to the Registrar that the motion to transfer the land was approved unanimously by both commonhold associations before it can be registered. If the transfer takes all of the commonhold land from a commonhold, then that commonhold will be dissolved.

Any rights or liabilities associated with the land before it was transferred will remain.

Frequently asked questions

What is enlargement of a commonhold?

Enlargement of a commonhold occurs when the amount of land comprising a commonhold changes. It can occur when land is added to a commonhold or where two commonholds merge into one.

Can a commonhold also be reduced in size?

Yes, a commonhold can reduce in size via the process of partial termination, which is subject to a variety of legal safeguards.

Partial termination may be used when the commonhold wishes to sell off part of the land as it is no longer required, or the commonhold needs to raise additional funds from the sale.

This requires unanimous support from members of the association, or in cases where this is not achieved the court have discretion over whether to approve the partial termination.

Compulsory purchase of commonhold land

The Bill contains provisions whose intent and purpose have been carried over from the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Act 2002, but they have received adjustments in order to improve their clarity and function alongside provisions in this Bill.

This includes a provision relating to the compulsory purchase of commonhold land, and how the land should be registered upon a compulsory purchase. This would require a compulsory purchase order to be granted, allowing a public authority to acquire the land without the consent of the owner, and is typically used when that authority requires the land for a project that serves the public interest. Compulsory purchases are not unique to commonhold land, and occur relatively rarely. They are also subject to regulations which must be followed, including the requirement for a government minister to confirm the compulsory purchase order.

Frequently asked questions

What is a compulsory purchase order?

A Compulsory Purchase Order (or CPO) is a legal function exercised by various authorities in the UK to acquire land or property without the consent of the owner, for public benefit or development projects.

Can a commonhold association reject a compulsory purchase?

If a compulsory purchase order is made it does not require the consent of the land owner (the commonhold association in the case of the common parts, and unit owners in the case of their individual units).

Unit owners do have the right to object and to challenge the decision. If the compulsory purchase order is confirmed, then unit owners do not have a further chance to appeal but do receive compensation for the land acquired.

See further compulsory purchase guidance.

Part 2: New leasehold flats: Moving to commonhold as the default for new flats

Today, where new flats are offered for sale, this is invariably on a leasehold basis (a long lease of over 21 years). The government wants that to change. As part of this legislation, government is reforming the commonhold system so that it will be a viable, workable and preferred alternative to the leasehold tenure. With these reforms in place, the government can see no good reason why, other than in exceptional circumstances, new flats should not be sold as commonhold.

Part 2 of the Bill places a statutory restriction on the grant or assignment of a long lease of a new flat. From the date this part of the Bill comes into effect, the marketing and grant of long leases on new flats will be prohibited. The intended effect is that all new flats for homeownership will have to be sold as commonhold, rather than leasehold, unless the lease qualifies for an exemption to the ban.

To protect consumers, those selling a qualifying exempt leasehold flat will need to be explicit during the marketing, sale and registration process that they are selling a leasehold flat and provide clear evidence of why the lease is a permitted lease. The mis-selling of a leasehold flat will entitle the consumer to redress, allowing them in most cases to acquire the flat as a commonhold flat, at no additional expense.

Existing leasehold flats will not be caught by the ban. The regrant of a lease for an existing leasehold flat, such as for a lease variation or extension, will also not be banned.

Following the Moving to Commonhold consultation, the government has confirmed its intention to bring the leasehold ban into force on a single date, following two and a half years after legislation for the reformed commonhold model has come into force. This will give consumers and the property sector time to become familiar with the new model and prepare for its use as the default tenure. To protect delivery of new housing supply and avoid disrupting live projects, developments for which a planning application has been made or planning consent granted before the ban commences will be able to continue selling new flats as leasehold under transitional arrangements. New projects brought forward after commencement of the ban will be required to use commonhold for the sale of flats, unless they qualify for a specified exemption.

We cannot pre-empt the parliamentary process, but it is the intention that the new commonhold model will be available for use before the end of this Parliament in 2029, following secondary legislation.

Alongside introduction of the Bill, we have also published our Direction of Travel plan. This sets out the implementation activities that are already underway to support the move to commonhold. In addition, the UK government will establish a Commonhold Implementation Steering Group chaired by the Housing Minister and comprising representatives of both industry and consumers. The group will help inform the development of the government’s Implementation Roadmap, which will be published closer to Royal Assent of the Bill, as well as working across the sector to support the development of sector-led information, guidance and support.

Frequently asked questions

Why are you banning the sale of leasehold flats?

Problems with leasehold have been well documented over recent years and deny leaseholders the full benefits of homeownership. There is an inherent power imbalance between the millions of leasehold homeowners and their landlords, who have almost full control and say over the upkeep and management of their homes and the charges they pay. The leaseholder experience is further undermined by depreciating lease terms, the threat of forfeiture, unjustified and onerous ground rents and the conditions for exploitative practices such as unjustified fees and charges.

This Bill will put in place a better alternative to leasehold, commonhold. In future, consumers will benefit from freehold homeownership and control over their own homes.

With the reformed commonhold in place, the government can see no reason why new flats should continue to be offered as leasehold, and so other than in exceptional circumstances, we are banning the sale of new leasehold flats. Commonhold will therefore become the default tenure for the ownership of new flats.

Why not mandate share of freehold instead of commonhold?

Share of freehold offers some benefits over traditional leasehold, as it allows homeowners to own their flats without a third-party landlord and gives them a greater degree of control.

However, owners in a share of freehold are still bound by the terms of their lease which depreciates over time and cannot be easily changed (e.g. if owners wanted to change how the building was used, such as to allow or ban short holiday lets, or to make improvements to the building such as seek agreement for and contributions towards solar panels or new electric vehicle chargers). While there is no third-party landlord, a small number of resident directors in a share of freehold assume the role of landlord and are not required to involve other homeowners in decision making about the running of the building.

Commonhold has been specifically designed for the ownership and management of shared buildings without a third-party landlord. It offers ownership that lasts forever and provides much more control over a building as it gives all owners the opportunity of a say over key decisions, such as setting the annual budget, and has much greater flexibility to change local rules or make changes to the building to meet the changing needs of a building or its owners over time.

When will the ban be switched on?

We cannot pre-empt the parliamentary process, but it is the intention that the new commonhold model will be available for use before the end of this Parliament in 2029, following secondary legislation.

The government has confirmed its intention to bring the leasehold ban into force on a single date, following two and a half years after legislation for the reformed commonhold model has come into force.

We know that the property industry will need time to adapt to the new commonhold model, and this period will allow the sector to prepare for commonhold to become the default tenure for new flats for sale.

Why won’t the ban come in sooner?

Respondents to the Moving to Commonhold consultation and evidence provided to the HCLG Select Committee as part of its pre-legislative scrutiny of the draft Bill were divided on the timing of the ban.

Consumers generally required minimal transitional time and favoured limited or no transitional arrangements for sites under development at the point of ban commencement. The property industry by comparison generally required longer to prepare for commonhold - from familiarisation with the new regime to updating IT systems and processes as well as offering new products, and favoured more generous transitional provisions for sites under development.

We have sought to strike the right balance of moving at pace, but also providing appropriate time for industry to prepare for use of the new commonhold regime at scale.

Will banning use of leasehold for new flats cause disruption to the housing market?

The UK government wants to support a smooth transition to commonhold, improving homeownership without reducing or slowing the delivery of new homes.

Recognising that the shift to commonhold is a significant change, we intend to allow two and a half years between the reformed commonhold framework becoming fully operational and the ban taking effect. This will allow time for those involved in the development of new flats to become familiar with the new commonhold regime, and if necessary, to make preparations for its use ahead of the leasehold ban coming into force. Developments where a planning application was made or granted before the ban takes effect will be permitted to continue selling new leasehold flats until those projects are complete.

Together, these provisions will protect existing live sites and development pipelines while ensuring that new projects brought forward after commencement of the ban use commonhold by default.

Won’t these transitional arrangements mean people will be subject to leasehold arrangements long into the future?

This is a major change to how people own their homes, and so it is right that we proceed with care. The government wants to ensure a smooth transition to commonhold without disrupting the delivery of new much needed housing already in the pipeline. That is why existing planning applications made and consents given prior to the ban will be permissible to be exempt from the ban, though a developer can of course choose to use commonhold for such sites if they wish.

New leasehold flats provided under these transitional arrangements will need to be offered to consumers with lease terms of 990 years where the developer owns the land on a freehold, and at the maximum term available to them if they only own the land on a lease. Coupled with existing restrictions on charging of ground rent on new leasehold properties, and our wider reforms to enfranchisement, these conditions will make it easier for homeowners to convert to commonhold if in future they wish to.

After the ban has commenced, any developers submitting new planning applications for blocks of flats for sale will have to sell them as commonhold unless they qualify for a specified exemption from the ban.

What are you doing to support the implementation of commonhold and readiness for the ban?

To ensure the new commonhold model can be used as soon as the necessary secondary regulations come into force, the government is already working with key delivery partners including HM Land Registry, HM Courts & Tribunals Service, Companies House, and the Leasehold Advisory Service (LEASE) to ensure that the supporting infrastructure and processes needed for the greater use of commonhold are available on day one of the new model being available for use. This also includes consideration of the information, guidance, and support that consumers will require from government delivery partners to successfully navigate the new regime.

To support both consumers and industry to prepare for the optional use of reformed commonhold, and its use by default following the commencement of the ban, the UK government will publish an Implementation Roadmap closer to Royal Assent of the Bill. This will set out a timetable for the necessary secondary legislation as well as wider support and guidance that will be made available for consumers and industry.

Alongside introduction of the Bill, we have also published our Direction of Travel plan. This sets out the implementation activities that are already underway to support the move to commonhold.

In addition, the UK government will establish a Commonhold Implementation Steering Group chaired by the Housing Minister and comprising representatives of both industry and consumers. The group will help inform the development of the government’s ‘Implementation Roadmap’ as well as working across the sector to support the development of sector-led information, guidance and support.

Scope of the ban on leasehold for new flats

Where flats can be provided as commonhold, the government believes that they should be. The Bill therefore introduces a broad ban on the use of new residential long leases for flats, covering different scenarios where a flat might come onto the market. This includes:

the development of a new block of flats to be sold partly or fully as homes for homeownership

a house newly converted into flats, where at least one flat is for sale on a long lease;

Commercial buildings newly redeveloped to contain flats, where at least one flat is for sale (for example, retail or office space with flats on upper floors)

purpose-built rental blocks whose owners have later opted to sell flats for homeownership (for example, a block entirely made up of Build to Rent flats where one or all flats are subsequently marketed for sale to prospective homeowners); and

other residential buildings where there are no existing flats with long residential leases at the time the ban comes into force (for example, an existing block of flats in vacant possession, that is refurbished so the flats can be resold)

Owners of existing leasehold flats will be unaffected by the ban. Landlords will continue to be able to grant new or replacement leases for existing leasehold flats, including where a lease is extended, varied or surrendered and regranted, or where a previous lease has expired, been voluntarily surrendered or terminated due to a breach of its terms. These arrangements are entered into voluntarily by existing leaseholders and their landlords.

There are limited exemptions in the Bill for situations where leasehold remains necessary or appropriate. As detailed in Permitted leases in a commonhold, some long leases will be permitted within a commonhold. These include: shared ownership leases; certain home finance arrangements, including home reversion plans (a form of equity release) and arrangements used for Islamic finance; non-assignable lifetime leases; and Grenfell Assisted Home Ownership leases.

The Bill also allows leasehold to continue outside commonhold in certain defined circumstances. These include: community land trusts; qualifying housing-with-care for older people; certain shared ownership and other housing schemes; and flats on National Trust, Crown or agricultural land. There are also exemptions for Grenfell Assisted Home Ownership, certain land subject to historic arrangements or compulsory purchase, and leases granted under the Right to Buy and Right to Acquire. These exemptions reflect the outcome of the Moving to Commonhold consultation, and further detail on exemptions can be found in the government response to the consultation.

Frequently asked questions

Why haven’t you banned the sale of all existing leasehold flats?

Banning existing leasehold flats would severely impact on the rights of leaseholders and their landlords. Instead, we are making it easier for people to convert their existing leasehold building to commonhold, should they wish to do so.

Why does the ban include existing buildings?

The ban is designed to apply to new leasehold flats. That means newly built flats but also covers other routes by which flats come onto the market for the first time, such as when existing houses are converted into flats, offices are converted into flats, or flats that were only for rent are then sold to homeowners.

We think this strikes the right balance between stopping the unnecessary creation of new leasehold flats, while allowing existing leaseholders to convert to commonhold if they wish to. This topic is also covered in the Moving to Commonhold consultation, and we would welcome feedback on it.

Which types of development will be exempt from the ban?

We sought views on the scope of the ban and the case for any exemptions through the Moving to Commonhold consultation.

The government has carefully considered responses to the consultation and has provided limited exemptions where leasehold remains necessary or appropriate. Some types of long lease will be permitted within commonhold. These include shared ownership leases; certain home finance arrangements, including home reversion plans (a form of equity release) and arrangements used for Islamic finance; non-assignable lifetime leases; and Grenfell Assisted Home Ownership leases.

There are also circumstances where leasehold flats will be permitted outside commonhold. These include community land trusts; qualifying housing-with-care for older people; certain shared ownership and other housing schemes; and flats on National Trust, Crown or agricultural land. There are also exemptions for Grenfell Assisted Home Ownership, certain land subject to historic arrangements or compulsory purchase, and leases granted under the Right to Buy and Right to Acquire.

Further detail about the exemptions and why they have been provided can be found in the government response to the consultation.

How will I know if my flat is captured by the ban?

The ban will only apply to new flats after the ban comes into effect. If your flat was already leasehold before the ban starts, you are unaffected by the ban and can still sell or extend your lease as normal.

To give buyers and their advisers certainty about buying new flats after the leasehold ban has commenced, the Bill sets out the compliance processes. For new flats sold as leasehold after the ban comes into force, there will be checks at different stages of the buying process. If a flat is exempt from the ban, any marketing materials will need to make clear that it is being sold as leasehold and why it is exempt. Before contracts are exchanged, the seller will need to provide the buyer with a warning notice explaining the exemption and supporting evidence. A prescribed statement must be included in the lease confirming that it complies with the ban, which will be checked when the lease is registered with HM Land Registry.

These checks are intended to give buyers and their conveyancers clear information about when and why a new flat is being sold as leasehold rather than commonhold, and to identify any problems before the transaction is completed.

Will specialist older people’s housing be exempt from the ban?

The government recognises the important role specialist older people’s housing plays in supporting people to live independently, and we want to support a diverse and sustainable sector.

Specialist older people’s housing ranges from relatively simple age-restricted housing to “housing-with-care” with extensive services and ongoing operator involvement. A one size fits all approach would therefore, not be appropriate.

Where new age-restricted homes are offered for sale, they will be provided as commonhold, and we will adapt commonhold to work effectively for more service-led forms of older people’s housing, giving residents the benefit of freehold ownership, greater transparency and control.

Housing-with-care, including Integrated Retirement Communities (IRCs), will be exempt from the ban, reflecting its care and support offer and more complex operational and funding arrangements. These schemes will be able to be developed as either leasehold or commonhold.

Further detail on the scope of the exemption is set out in the government response to the consultation.

Enforcement and redress

The ban on the use of leasehold for new flats will be supported by a clear system of checks and remedies. This framework is designed to protect consumers, ensure compliance by developers and landlords, and provide backstop rights to correct any breach of the ban.

How compliance with the ban will be checked:

Marketing: Advertising a new leasehold flat will not be permitted unless the lease qualifies for an exemption. Where an exemption applies, marketing materials must clearly state the basis for that exemption.

Sale: Before contracts are exchanged, the seller must issue a ‘warning notice’ for any exempt leasehold flat. This notice will explain why the exemption applies and provide supporting evidence.

Registration: A prescribed statement must be included in the lease confirming that it complies with the ban, which will be checked when the lease is registered with HM Land Registry. If this statement is missing, a temporary restriction will be placed on the title, preventing resale until the issue is resolved.

If a leasehold flat is sold in breach of the ban, the consumer will have statutory redress rights. Remedies will vary depending on the nature of the breach:

Lease unlawfully granted in a commonhold building: The leaseholder will typically have the right to acquire the flat as a commonhold unit, at no cost to them.

Lease unlawfully granted in a relevant building outside commonhold: Leaseholders will typically have the right to require the building to be converted to commonhold and to acquire their flat as a commonhold unit, at no cost to them.

Missing evidence for an exemption: If an exemption applies or the lease was not caught by the ban, but the required prescribed statement was not provided, the leaseholder will have the right to have this corrected in the lease at the landlord’s expense.

Right to terminate a lease: in very limited circumstances, where the other redress routes are not available, consumers will have a right to terminate a lease that has been granted in breach of the ban and to seek compensation. This provides an alternative form of redress where conversion to commonhold is not appropriate or not possible.

If the landlord or freeholder does not comply with the remedy, the matter can be referred to the tribunal.

The Bill gives local authorities powers to enforce the ban. They will have the power to issue financial penalties for non-compliance with fines ranging from £500 to £30,000 per breach, scaled to reflect the level of consumer harm. To ensure consistency and effective enforcement, a lead enforcement authority will be appointed by the Secretary of State.

Frequently asked questions

How will a buyer know whether a leasehold flat is exempt from the ban?

Where a flat is exempt from the ban, the seller will need to make this clear to the buyer and provide evidence showing why the exemption applies.

The Bill includes checks at different stages of the transaction. Marketing materials for an exempt leasehold flat will need to make clear that it is being sold as leasehold and the basis on which it is exempt.

Before contracts are exchanged, the seller will be required to provide the buyer with a warning notice explaining why the exemption applies and supporting evidence.

A prescribed statement must be included in the lease confirming that it complies with the ban, which will be checked when the lease is registered with HM Land Registry. Together, these requirements are intended to give buyers and their conveyancers clear information about why a new flat is being sold as leasehold rather than commonhold, and to identify problems before the transaction is completed.

Would consumers have to pay their own legal costs for exercising their rights to redress?

The legislation is designed so that consumers are not penalised for enforcing their rights. If a consumer is mis-sold a prohibited lease, the remedies available to them such as acquiring the flat as a commonhold unit or requiring the building to convert to commonhold should be at no overall cost to the consumer.

Ultimately, the costs of a successful claim should be borne by the party responsible (i.e. the freeholder or landlord), with buyers being entitled to recover their costs.

Who will enforce the ban?

The Bill enables the Secretary of State to appoint a lead enforcement authority to oversee enforcement of the ban, provide guidance to local areas, and to investigate and take enforcement action on their behalf.

The Bill also provides that local trading standards authorities will have powers to enforce the ban on new leasehold flats. They will be able to investigate breaches and issue financial penalties for non-compliance.

We will confirm who the lead enforcement authority will be in due course.

Do you think £30,000 is enough to deter a seller?

The £30,000 maximum penalty per breach is designed to be a strong deterrent and aligns with penalties in the ban on new leasehold houses (in the LFRA 2024). The total amount can rise substantially if multiple breaches are committed, for example where multiple flats in the same building are mis-sold.

Importantly, financial penalties are only one part of the enforcement framework. Sellers who break the rules may also face other consequences, such as statutory rights for buyers to require conversion to commonhold at the freeholder’s expense. Taken together, these measures are designed to make non-compliance highly unattractive.

What if a seller breaches the ban by accident?

The ban is designed with multiple safeguards to prevent unintentional breaches. There will be clear rules at the marketing, sale and registration stages, so vendors and their advisers have several opportunities to check compliance before a transaction completes.

Where a breach nevertheless occurs, consumers will have individual redress rights to put matters right and the seller may face additional civil enforcement action.

Part 3: Leasehold enfranchisement and extension

Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act fixes

The Bill makes the amendments to the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024 to correct a small number of specific but serious flaws which prevent certain provisions from operating correctly.

The amendments which address the flaws, alongside the necessary secondary legislation which is being completed in parallel to this Bill, will enable the LFRA 2024’s leasehold enfranchisement reforms to be implemented. Once in force, the enfranchisement reforms will make it easier and cheaper for leaseholders to extend their lease or purchase their freehold.

The corrections in the Bill close a loophole in the valuation scheme and make clarifications to support the intended application of the valuation methodology. Amendments also clarify the operation of landlords’ existing redevelopment break rights, permit certain costs of third parties involved in enfranchisement to be claimed and remove the ability to agree restrictions on further enfranchisement or lease extension claims following the voluntary withdrawal of a claim relating to a flat. A few inaccurate cross references are corrected and consequential amendments are made to ensure the provisions in the LFRA 2024 can be implemented smoothly.

Frequently asked questions

When will the LFRA’s enfranchisement reforms be implemented?

The government is acting to provide homeowners with greater rights, powers and protections over their homes by implementing the LFRA as quickly as possible. This will require an extensive programme of secondary legislation.

We intend to commence the enfranchisement reforms as soon as possible after the Bill’s Royal Assent.

The parts of the LFRA which can be commenced quickly, have been implemented. Provisions came into force on 24 July 2024 relating to rentcharge arrears, building safety legal costs and the work of professional insolvency practitioners. On 31 October 2024, the government commenced further building safety measures. On 31 January 2025, provisions to remove the 2-year qualifying rule in relation to enfranchisement and lease extensions came into force, and on 3 March 2025, the Right to Manage provisions (expanding access, reforming its costs and voting rights) came into force.

What about the new extension rights for shared ownership leaseholders?

We intend to commence the LFRA reforms for all leaseholders, including shared ownership leaseholders, as soon as possible after the Bill’s Royal Assent.

We have been clear we will correct the omission that would deny tens of thousands of shared ownership leaseholders the right to extend their lease with their direct landlord where the providers do not have sufficiently long leases to grant 990 year extensions which will be addressed in this Bill.

What is the “loophole” in the valuation methodology?

The valuation scheme contains a loophole which means some people or organisations could avoid paying the correct price for their lease extension or freehold acquisition. To protect the integrity of the new valuation methodology, the Bill inserts anti-avoidance provisions in new Schedule 4A into the LFRA 2024 to prevent the new valuation scheme from being compromised.

The anti-avoidance provisions set out how the price of the freehold or lease extension will be calculated where there has been a deliberate attempt to exploit the valuation scheme.

The provisions take account of the circumstances of the transaction and the connections between those involved and the leaseholder making the claim to specifically target arrangements intended to manipulate the valuation scheme to gain a benefit from a price-reduction.

The Bill makes further amendments to Schedule 4 to ensure the valuation scheme operates as it was intended: - to counteract the effect of transactions intended to increase the share of the payment received for a freehold purchase or lease extension by increasing a share of the market value. In these cases, the increased share can be reduced and redistributed appropriately between other share owners - when a leaseholder buys their freehold or lease extension, the standard valuation method is not compulsory to establish the price if their lease was granted from a lease that had itself been granted in return for payment of a modern ground rent - in these cases, as the extended lease was granted at a modern ground rent for the extension period, the landlord did not receive a premium. The amendment ensures that the valuation scheme is not applied in a way that disregards the value of that modern ground rent

Where the price of a freehold or leasehold extension, or the share of the price meets the criteria for a price adjustment to be made, the Bill provides that the result must be just and equitable.

Why have you closed the loophole in the valuation scheme?

The valuation “loophole” arises from the inadvertent operation of the valuation scheme that goes far beyond the intended reforms.

The LFRA’s combined enfranchisement reforms which together make it easier and cheaper for leaseholders to buy their freehold or lease extension are intended to balance leaseholders’ interests with those of freeholders.

Under the new valuation scheme, when leaseholders extend their leases or acquire the freehold to their homes, it was intended that they would pay for the value of the landlord’s ground rent income (where payable), subject to the cap under that scheme, and the landlord’s reversion (their right to have the property back when the lease expires). The “loophole” means some individuals or organisations could gain an unintended advantage.

To overcome this problem, the Bill inserts anti-avoidance provisions into the LFRA 2024.

What happens if a new “loophole” is found in the valuation scheme?

The Bill gives the Secretary of State power to amend the anti-avoidance provisions by regulations.

This will ensure that the government can respond quickly to address developments which may evolve over time to undermine the integrity of the valuation scheme.

Any provisions made by the regulations are subject to approval by Parliament.

Third party process costs

Once the relevant provisions of the LFRA 2024 are commenced, each party to an enfranchisement, lease extension or ground rent buy out claim will have to pay their own non-litigation or ‘process’ costs, for example for conveyancing and valuation fees, unless one of a limited number of exceptions applies.

The Bill amends the relevant provisions in the Leasehold Reform Act 1967, the Leasehold Reform, Housing and Urban Development Act 1993 and the LFRA 2024 to create a further exception to the rule that each party pays their own process costs to provide that certain third parties to leases (not being the landlord or leaseholder), such as resident-led management organisations, are able to recover their process costs where they have no other means of meeting them. Without this change, an unintended outcome from the reforms requiring each party to pay their own process costs could put these organisations at risk of insolvency.

The amendments give the Secretary of State, in relation to England, and the Welsh Minister, in relation to Wales, powers to specify in regulations which third parties can recover process costs, the circumstances in which leaseholders must contribute and how much they must pay. The appropriate tribunal can decide what costs may be recovered by the third party, where the parties cannot agree whether a payment is due or the amount payable.

The provisions also ensure these process costs are treated consistently with similar costs so that they are not taken into account for the purposes of Stamp Duty Land Tax.

Redevelopment break rights

The Bill corrects an unintended constraint on landlords’ existing redevelopment break rights that applies in certain limited circumstances where there are complex chains of leases.

Freeholders have rights to end leases in their building in order to redevelop it when a building comes to the end of its life. These rights allow a landlord, in limited circumstances and during specified time windows, to apply to the court to terminate an extended lease where this is needed for redevelopment.

A landlord must prove to a court that redevelopment is necessary within a time period “window” and pay compensation to leaseholders if their lease is terminated.

The redevelopment “break rights” only apply at limited time windows during the term of a lease. The Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024 adjusts the break windows to reflect the new 990-year lease extension terms to broadly the last 12 months of the original lease or the last five years of each period of 90 years of the extension.

Schedule 16 of the Bill amends the law governing break rights under the Leasehold Reform Act 1967 and the Leasehold Reform, Housing and Urban Development Act 1993 to clarify how the rights work where a sub-leaseholder obtains a lease extension and the break windows may not align.

Amendments in the Bill also clarify affected leaseholders’ rights to receive an appropriate share of the compensation and take part in proceedings, for example if they wish to contest a freeholder’s claim to use the break rights.

Frequently asked questions

Can a freeholder automatically get their property back during one of the redevelopment break right windows?

To use the break right, a freeholder must make an application to the court for an order terminating the lease on the grounds of redevelopment.

A freeholder may only take possession of the building if a court accepts their evidence that redevelopment is genuinely required. This may be because the building is at the end of its useful life and needs to be demolished or needs significant work to renovate it.

Having assessed the evidence, including hearing any views from affected leaseholders, if the court accepts the claim, it will grant an order for possession and the freeholder must pay the affected leaseholder compensation.

The compensation paid to leaseholders is calculated by reference to the amount which the extended lease could be sold for and assumes that the lease gives vacant possession.

The amendment ensures that compensation must be calculated by reference to the value of the longest lease that has been terminated.

What about agreements to restrict extension and freehold purchase claims?

The LFRA 2024 removed the ability for landlords and tenants of houses to make an agreement that the tenant would make no further claims for a set period, when the tenant had voluntarily withdrawn their enfranchisement claim.

The Bill makes the same provision for tenants of flats so that all tenants, irrespective of the type of property they occupy, are protected from pressure to agree to waive their right to buy their freehold or extend their lease.

Why were leaseholders of houses protected against agreements to waive their enfranchisement rights, but not flats?

There was no intention to retain these types of agreements for leaseholders of flats.

The amendment corrects the inadvertent omission so that leaseholders of flats and houses cannot be bound by voluntary agreements to waive their right to claim enfranchisement after withdrawing a previous claim.

Part 4: Regulation of leaseholder and estate management

Ground Rent

The Leasehold Reform (Ground Rent) Act 2022 (“GRA 2022”) set ground rents for most new residential leases at a peppercorn. The Bill amends the GRA 2022 to cap ground rents for leases granted before the commencement of that Act at £250 a year, changing to a peppercorn (effectively zero) after 40 years. It will apply to existing long leases (exceeding 21 years) for a single dwelling with a few limited exceptions.

This will deliver the government’s manifesto commitment to “tackle unregulated and unaffordable ground rent charges”.

The Bill also amends existing legislation to specify how the landlord must give notice to a leaseholder in order to collect ground rent under a lease; how third-party costs are paid in relation to ground rent buy out (GRBO) rights; and to provide the tribunal with additional powers in relation to GRBO claims.

Frequently asked questions

What is ground rent?

Ground rents are an annual or periodic charge that leaseholders are obliged to pay to freeholders under the terms of their lease. Unlike a service charge, there is no requirement to provide a service in return for this payment.

When will the £250 cap be in place?

The ground rent cap will be in place when the measures in the Bill and the necessary secondary legislation are commenced. The government aims to commence them six months after Royal Assent.

How does this affect leaseholders who currently pay less than £250 per year?

These proposals will result in savings for the overwhelming majority of residential leaseholders in England and Wales who pay ground rents.

If leaseholders pay ground rent which is less than £250 but is due to rise over time, it can never be more than £250 a year. After 40 years almost all ground rents will change to a peppercorn (effectively zero).

Why is the government reducing ground rents to a peppercorn after 40 years rather than immediately?

There is a clear, compelling case for government to intervene in ground rents given the harms they cause to leaseholders. Capping ground rents at £250 for the next 40 years will put an end to problems people face as a result when they are mortgaging, buying and selling leasehold properties. After 40 years, ground rents will be capped at a peppercorn (effectively zero).

This approach strikes a balance between the need to address high and escalating ground rents, and bring them to an end as soon as possible, whilst also considering the impacts on landlords, investors and the wider property market.

Will leaseholders actually be required to pay a peppercorn after 40 years?

A peppercorn ground rent is an annual rent of one peppercorn per year. The peppercorn preserves the conventional legal structure of a lease under which a rent is reserved, but ensures that the rent has no financial value.

In practice, landlords do not demand payment of a peppercorn.

Which properties will be exempt from the cap?

The Bill sets out a limited number of properties which will be exempt from the cap. These mirror the current approach of the GRA 2022. The Bill provides for exemptions covering business leases, community-led housing and home finance plans.

There is also provision for the treatment of shared ownership leases and lease extensions of houses made under the Leasehold Reform Act 1967.

Leases granted for no premium are not regulated by the GRA 2022. That is because they are analogous to long-term rental contacts and the full payment for occupying the home is the rental payment.

The government is continuing to consider the treatment of so-called ‘quid pro quo’ leases where people agree to pay a higher ground rent in return for a lower premium. The government consultation on this issue closed on 27 August 2026.

Administration charges

Administration charges arise where a lease or estate management arrangement requires a leaseholder or a homeowner of a managed dwelling on a freehold estate to pay fees to a landlord or estate manager for administrative matters, such as dealing with requests for permission to carry out works and providing standard documents.

The Bill allows the appropriate national authorities in England and Wales to make regulations setting the maximum amounts payable for specified administration charges. A maximum amount may be set at zero. Where a leaseholder or homeowner has paid more than the maximum amount, the leaseholder or homeowner may apply to the tribunal. The tribunal may order the recipient of the payment to repay the excess and may also order the person who demanded the charge to pay damages of up to £5,000 to the leaseholder or homeowner.

The provisions also allow for the tribunal to make orders varying leases, agreements and other documents that provide for leaseholders and homeowners to pay prohibited estate management administration charges.

Frequently asked questions

Which fees will actually be capped?

We will consult on which administration and permission fees are most appropriate for capping. The detailed design of the caps will be informed by evidence from leaseholders, homeowners, landlords, managing agents and wider stakeholders, before being implemented through secondary legislation.

When will the caps be implemented?

The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill includes powers to enable the Secretary of State in England and the Welsh Ministers in Wales to cap specified administration and permission fees.

We will undertake a public consultation to determine which fees should be capped, how any cap should operate and the appropriate level of caps. Once that work is complete, the caps will be implemented through secondary legislation.

Taking this approach ensures that the caps will be targeted, proportionate and based on evidence from consumers, landlords, managing agents and other stakeholders.

Gigabit-capable broadband connection

Leaseholders in a block of flats or other multi-dwelling buildings will be legally entitled to a response from the freeholder (or responsible person) with regard to a request to install a gigabit-capable broadband connection in their building. The measures address two practical barriers to deployment: difficulty in identifying the right party for telecoms operators to engage with, and a lack of response where that party has been identified.

A leaseholder’s request must reach the person responsible for the building, who must engage with relevant broadband operators and respond to the leaseholder within set timeframes, so that requests are not simply ignored. Their response will explain whether a connection is feasible or not, based on information from broadband providers, or set out any relevant plans for broadband deployment already underway.

This will help tackle deployment delays and improve transparency, while ensuring that any broadband installation still respects existing property rights and agreements. These measures do not give operators a right to install apparatus, do not require a landlord to agree to installation, and do not replace the Electronic Communications Code.

Frequently asked questions

How many households are actually affected, and how many will benefit directly from this intervention?

As of May 2026, there are c.1.13 million flats in England and Wales without gigabit-capable connectivity. This is 19% of the self-contained flats in England and Wales. By comparison only 11% of residential premises in England and Wales do not have a gigabit-capable connection.

Of the 1.13 million with a gigabit-capable connection, 633k are leasehold flats that currently do not have a gigabit-capable connection. An estimated 360k flats are not expected to have a gigabit capable connection by 2029 and could benefit from the leasehold legislative interventions.

MHCLG estimates that as of 2024/25 there are ~178k social housing leasehold premises in England, or 5.3% of all leasehold flats.

Advice about estate management

Homeowners on managed estates may face difficulty understanding estate management arrangements, scrutinising and challenging charges, obtaining information, holding estate managers to account and navigating routes to redress.

They should have access to clear, independent information and advice comparable to existing advice funded by the government for leaseholders, commonhold unit owners and owners of park homes.

The Bill gives the Secretary of State the power to fund free and independent advice services for homeowners living on privately managed estates, similar to the advice currently provided by the Leasehold Advisory Service (LEASE).

LEASE currently provides free information and advice to leaseholders, commonhold unit owners and park home owners in England and Wales, including on building safety issues.

This advice could help homeowners on managed estates understand their new rights and protections under the government‘s plans to bring into force measures in the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024. Before the end of this Parliament, the government is introducing a new regulatory framework to give homeowners on privately managed estates new rights, protections and powers to hold their estate manager to account for the money they spend. Details of the exact advice service provision will be agreed with the delivery partner.

Frequently asked questions

Who will this advice be for?

The government’s primary focus is assistance for freehold homeowners living on managed estates.

For example, estates are often managed by a resident management company. These are frequently run by volunteer directors who are themselves homeowners or residents. They may require support in understanding their responsibilities and obligations, particularly where they are managing communal services, levying charges, making decisions on behalf of residents, or overseeing managing agents.

Some estates are run by third-party management agents. In this case, homeowners may wish to seek advice to understand what steps they can take if they are unhappy with their managing agent.

However, the Bill does not strictly limit the advice to homeowners, as long as the matter concerns estate management arrangements.

What advice will this cover?

We expect that advice will cover fees and charges, restrictive covenants, estate rentcharges, management company governance and sales.

It is likely to also support understanding of the new regulatory framework for managed estates, which will be introduced before the end of this Parliament. This new framework includes provisions concerning estate management charges and administration charges, information rights, enforcement and applications to the appropriate tribunal.

Details of the exact service provision will be agreed with the delivery partner.

When will this advice be available?

The power will come into effect two months after Royal Assent and we expect a provider will start to deliver the service as soon as possible thereafter.

Part 5: Enforcement of long residential leases: abolishing forfeiture and introducing a fairer lease enforcement scheme

Currently, landlords can rely on a contractual right called forfeiture to terminate a lease if the leaseholder breaches its terms. This can result in a leaseholder losing their home and all the equity they have built up, even where the value of the property is far greater than the debt owed or harm caused by the breach. Although completed forfeitures are rare, the risk of losing the lease and all its value can itself place significant pressure on leaseholders.

The Bill abolishes forfeiture for long residential leases and replaces it with a statutory lease enforcement scheme. The new scheme will ensure that landlords can still take effective action where a leaseholder breaches their lease, while introducing stronger and more consistent safeguards for leaseholders. For all types of breach, leaseholders will receive information explaining the enforcement process and their rights, and notice of proposed enforcement action. They will then have a minimum of 28 days in which to remedy the breach before court action can be taken. This provides a clear minimum period and gives leaseholders more time to resolve matters than they might otherwise have had under forfeiture, where the requirement is only to allow a reasonable period in the circumstances. Once a breach has been finally determined or admitted, landlords will have 6 months to bring enforcement proceedings, preventing the threat of enforcement from remaining open-ended. If the breach remains unresolved, the landlord can apply to the court, which will determine the most appropriate and proportionate remedy in the circumstances. This could include requiring the breach to be remedied or, in the most serious cases, ordering the property to be sold. Unlike forfeiture, if the property is sold, the leaseholder will keep any money left after the relevant debts and costs have been paid.

Frequently asked questions

Why are you abolishing forfeiture?

Forfeiture is an outdated and disproportionate remedy. It can result in a leaseholder losing their home and all the equity they have built up, including for relatively minor breaches of their lease.

Although actual forfeitures are rare, the threat of losing everything can itself be used as powerful leverage.

We are therefore replacing forfeiture with a fairer enforcement scheme that preserves effective remedies for landlords while protecting leaseholders from losing everything.

How will the new lease enforcement scheme work?

Under the new lease enforcement scheme, landlords will no longer be able to end a lease unilaterally. If a breach occurs, they must meet certain statutory conditions designed to protect leaseholders and then they can apply to the court for a remedy. The court will decide the most appropriate and proportionate remedy, taking into account factors such as the seriousness of the breach, whether the breach can be put right and the conduct of the parties. Possible outcomes include an order requiring the leaseholder to remedy the breach or, in rarer cases, an order for sale of the property, with protections to ensure the leaseholder is compensated for any remaining equity.

If the court can still order a sale, isn’t this just forfeiture by another name?

Under forfeiture, the lease can be terminated and the leaseholder can lose both their home and all the equity they have built up.

Under the new scheme, an order for sale will be a court-led remedy. If a sale is ordered the proceeds will be applied to the relevant liabilities and the leaseholder will retain any remaining proceeds from the sale.

This ensures that where loss of the home is ultimately necessary to enforce a breach, it happens through a proportionate process without the leaseholder automatically losing the remaining value of their property.

Will landlords be able to use the scheme to enforce all breaches of lease?

Ground rent arrears will be excluded from the new scheme, as will other financial breaches below a specified threshold.

The threshold will be set in regulations following consultation, within a range specified in the Bill of £500 and £5,000.

Landlords will still be able to use ordinary civil debt recovery processes for debts which fall outside the scheme.

How will landlords still be able to protect other residents and ensure lease obligations are complied with?

Abolishing forfeiture does not remove leaseholders’ responsibility to pay service charges or comply with other obligations that support the proper management and maintenance of their building.

Landlords will retain effective enforcement powers. Where the statutory conditions are met, they can apply to the court for an appropriate remedy, including an order for sale in the most serious cases.

The Bill also provides for landlords to recover their reasonable litigation costs where the relevant conditions are met, ensuring they are not left unfairly out of pocket for taking necessary enforcement action.

The reform therefore changes the consequences and safeguards around enforcement, rather than removing landlords’ ability to enforce lease obligations.

Will the lease enforcement scheme apply to existing as well as new leases?

The scheme will apply to existing long residential leases where the landlord currently has a right of forfeiture, as well as to new long residential leases.

Applying the reforms only to new leases would leave existing leaseholders exposed to forfeiture potentially for many years because of the long duration of residential leases.

The reforms will not apply to commercial or agricultural leases, where forfeiture will continue to operate.

Part 6: Estate rentcharges: Regulation of remedies for arrears of estate rentcharges

Rentcharges are annual or periodic sums charged on land. One type of rentcharge, estate rentcharge, is commonly used on privately managed estates to recover the costs of maintaining shared amenities such as roads, drains and sewers, and activities such as landscaping open spaces and play areas.

Under current law, sections 121 and 122 of the Law of Property Act 1925 give rentcharge owners particularly severe enforcement powers if a homeowner falls behind on payments. These include taking possession of the property until the arrears are cleared, granting a lease of the property to trustees which can continue even after the arrears have been paid, and appointing a receiver with mortgagee-like powers. These remedies can be used for very small arrears and without notice being given to the homeowner. This can create serious problems for homeowners, including when they come to sell or remortgage their property. Mortgage lenders may also require costly deeds of variation to remove these risks before agreeing to lend.

The Bill repeals sections 121 and 122 of the Law of Property Act 1925, ending these disproportionate remedies. The repeal will apply to estate rentcharges and other limited categories of rentcharge which can still be created under section 2 of the Rentcharges Act 1977. It will not prevent legitimate arrears from being recovered. Rentcharge owners will continue to be able to recover unpaid sums through more proportionate means, which may include a debt claim in the county court, a claim for breach of covenant where the obligation is enforceable as a covenant, and any other lawful remedy available under the deed or agreement. The Bill will also introduce a new safeguard requiring homeowners to be given formal notice of the debt before proceedings or other prescribed enforcement action to recover the arrears may be commenced.

Frequently asked questions

What is an estate rentcharge?

A rentcharge is an annual or periodic sum charged on land.

An estate rentcharge is commonly used on privately managed estates to recover the costs of maintaining communal amenities such as roads, drains, sewers, open spaces and play areas.

Why are you changing the law?

The current remedies are outdated and disproportionate. They can be used after arrears have remained unpaid for 40 days, including where the amount owed is very small, without any general statutory requirement for advance notice to the homeowner. This creates uncertainty for homeowners and lenders and can increase the cost and complexity of buying, selling and remortgaging affected properties.

In Roberts v Lawton (2016), a rentcharge owner granted 99-year leases over properties for arrears of between £6 and £15, and demanded £650 plus VAT from one homeowner to surrender the lease. This demonstrates the disproportionate consequences these powers can have.

Repealing sections 121 and 122 will protect homeowners while ensuring that legitimate arrears can continue to be recovered using more proportionate remedies.

Who will benefit from these changes?

Homeowners will no longer face the risk that a rentcharge owner could take possession of their property or grant a lease over it because of arrears of a rentcharge.

Removing these powers should also give mortgage lenders greater confidence in lending on properties with estate rentcharges and reduce problems when homeowners sell or remortgage.

The changes should make the homebuying process simpler and reduce unnecessary costs for homeowners.

What evidence do you have to support these changes?

As part of the government’s consultation, Enhanced protections for homeowners on freehold estates, which closed on 12 March 2026, the government sought views on whether sections 121 and 122 of the Law of Property Act 1925 should be repealed for all rentcharges, including less common rentcharges created through family trusts, statutory schemes or court orders.

The responses demonstrated broad support for repeal and did not provide sufficient evidence for retaining the remedies in any of the circumstances considered.
